perspective:
From Sara Manuelito’s available perspective:

- Sara is a speech-language pathologist and long-time colleague/close friend of Shirley Whiteplume, a nurse; they have worked together at a community health center for several years.
- At a mutual patient’s funeral, Sara observes Shirley’s somber demeanor and suspects Shirley is deeply affected by the loss.
- Sara tells Shirley she saw how much Shirley cared for the patient. She hears Shirley say it has been tough and that she keeps thinking whether more could have been done. Sara responds that they did everything they could and recalls the good care and moments of joy they provided. Shirley says it is hard to let go.
- During a coffee break at work, Sara raises the patient’s treatment decisions because she senses Shirley feels burdened. Shirley says she feels responsible, wonders if pushing for a different approach might have helped, appreciates Sara’s words, and says it is hard to accept. Sara tells her they made the best decisions with the information they had and that the burden is too heavy to carry alone.
- In a quiet office moment, Sara observes Shirley’s continued reserved behavior and minimal emotional expression. Sara confronts her, saying she has noticed Shirley holding back feelings and that it is okay to be open. Shirley says she does not want to seem unprofessional or weak. Sara says showing emotion does not make her weak and is healthy among friends. Shirley says maybe Sara is right and she will try to be more open.
- Later, Sara feels her previous confrontation may have been too harsh and apologizes. Shirley says it was a bit much but knows Sara meant well and appreciates the apology. Sara says she is there for Shirley in whatever way she needs. Shirley thanks her and says they should keep talking because it helps.
- After some time, Sara notices Shirley seems improved and feels hopeful. She asks how Shirley is feeling. Shirley says she feels better thanks to their talks and Sara’s support. Sara offers to spend more time together outside work; Shirley agrees and suggests planning something for the weekend.
- Sara does not have access to Shirley’s private internal state beyond what Shirley states aloud and what Sara observes or infers.
